title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 2: For or Against GMA
keywords: the first of a thousand steps
aspire for credibility, first and foremost
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's September 30, 2007 Inquirer column answering readers who, after his earlier 'GMA's Legacy' piece, demanded to know whether he was for or against the President

His defining stance that he writes 'for or against causes, actions and principles, not pro or contra persons and personalities' -- 'interested in what wins, not in who wins,' impugning the crime but not detesting the criminal ('we hate sin but not the sinner')

His diagnosis that GMA's worst failing is in transparent and accountable governance, costing her credibility (a 'minus 11' SWS trust rating; the Philippines falling from 121st to 131st of 180 in Transparency International's corruption index)

A balanced ledger on the rebounding economy -- crediting both the OFWs' record remittances and GMA's reforms (EVAT, privatization, mining, tourism, the stock market, 7.5% growth) -- capped by the 'cancer patient' analogy that a distrusted leader is blamed even for the necessary pain of the cure, so credibility must come 'first and foremost'
sub_topics: The provocation: a 'pointed, even sarcastic' reader asked how CJP, whose Court 'dealt successive blows to GMA,' could still want the President to succeed -- had he not joined the anti-GMA movement?

The jurist's stance: trained to rule for or against petitions, not parties, he writes 'for or against causes, actions and principles, not pro or contra persons,' is 'interested in what wins, not in who wins,' and 'we hate sin but not the sinner' -- and offers solutions, not just criticism

GMA's worst failing -- transparency and accountability: a long-low trust rating (a 'dismal minus 11' in the September 24 SWS survey), a public impression of widespread graft, and the country's fall from 121st to 131st of 180 in Transparency International's corruption rating

His standing remedies: direct relatives, officials and cronies to follow the Constitution and anti-graft, ethics and procurement laws; and fortify democratic institutions with trustworthy Supreme Court and Comelec appointees -- 'with prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law'

The rebounding economy (the 'bright-lined' area): the budget deficit arrested, foreign borrowing reduced, interest and inflation at lows, the peso stronger -- even if 'not an economist,' he can feel the indicators

Crediting the OFWs vs. GMA: the overseas Filipino workers who remitted '$14 billion last year -- double that sent five years ago' are 'the real heroes,' but GMA's push for the expanded VAT (EVAT), privatization (especially power), large-scale mining, tourism and the stock market 'cannot be brushed aside'; growth hit a record 7.5% in Q2
The EVAT backlash: consumers 'pillory' her for higher VAT on oil products, and the senatorial defeat of her candidates (Ralph Recto, Mike Defensor) was widely blamed on EVAT

The 'myth' rebuttal and the cancer-patient analogy: critics say the recovery is a 'statistical hocus-pocus' the poor don't feel; CJP answers with 'the first of a thousand steps' (Korea, Singapore, China needed years), then argues a trusted leader's people 'will willingly suffer transitory torment' like a patient who trusts a physician through chemotherapy -- while a distrusted leader is mocked even for the pain of the remedy (as in India, where the reformers were voted out and their opponents reaped the prosperity)

stances.claim: He is neither for nor against GMA the person: as a jurist he is 'for or against causes, actions and principles, not pro or contra persons,' 'interested in what wins, not in who wins,' impugning the crime but not detesting the criminal -- so wanting the President to succeed and criticizing her failings are not contradictory.
stances.rhetorical_move: issues-not-persons distinction: dissolving the for/against-her framing by separating the merits of actions from loyalty to a personality

stances.claim: GMA's gravest failing is the collapse of transparent and accountable governance -- evidenced by a 'minus 11' trust rating and the country's slide to 131st of 180 on corruption -- even though the rebounding economy (to which both the OFWs' $14B remittances and her EVAT/privatization/mining reforms contributed, yielding 7.5% growth) is the bright spot.
stances.rhetorical_move: balanced ledger: pairing a candid economic credit with an unsparing credibility debit to keep the appraisal even-handed

stances.claim: Credibility must come 'first and foremost,' because a people who trust their leader 'will willingly suffer transitory torment' (like a patient who trusts a physician through chemotherapy), while a distrusted leader is mocked even for the necessary pain of the cure -- as India's reformers learned when they were voted out and their opponents reaped the prosperity.
stances.rhetorical_move: cancer-patient analogy plus cautionary example: making the abstract value of trust vivid and showing its political cost when absent

notable_anecdotes: The sarcastic reader: CJP opens with a reader's jab -- that after his Court 'dealt successive blows to GMA,' he had surely 'joined... the anti-GMA movement' -- which he uses to explain why he judges issues, not persons.

The cancer patient and chemotherapy: his signature analogy holds that a patient who trusts the physician endures the debilitation of chemotherapy without resentment, just as a people who trust their leader will bear 'transitory torment' for eventual healing -- but the distrusted leader is blamed for both the disease and the cure.
$14 billion in remittances: he singles out the OFWs, who remitted '$14 billion last year -- double that sent five years ago,' as 'the real heroes' of the upturn, while still crediting GMA's reforms.

India's ungrateful turn: he recalls that India's reformers 'who prescribed the painful medicine were booted out of power,' while the politicians who opposed them 'were voted in to revel in the prosperity started by the hated reformers' -- a warning about governing without credibility.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) is CJP's September 30, 2007 Inquirer column responding to readers who, after his 'GMA's Legacy' piece, demanded to know whether he was for or against the President -- one sarcastically suggesting he had joined the anti-GMA movement. He answers that, as a jurist trained to rule for or against petitions rather than parties, he writes 'for or against causes, actions and principles, not pro or contra persons,' is 'interested in what wins, not in who wins,' and impugns the crime without detesting the criminal ('we hate sin but not the sinner'). GMA's worst failing, he says, is the collapse of transparent and accountable governance, which has wrecked her credibility -- a 'dismal minus 11' SWS trust rating and the country's fall from 121st to 131st of 180 on Transparency International's corruption index -- and his standing remedies are to hold her circle to the anti-graft and ethics laws and to fortify the Supreme Court and Comelec. He then credits the economy as the 'bright-lined' area: the deficit arrested, interest and inflation low, the peso stronger, with both the OFWs' record '$14 billion' in remittances ('the real heroes') and GMA's reforms -- the expanded VAT, privatization, mining, tourism and a resurgent stock market -- driving a record 7.5% second-quarter growth, even as consumers pillory her for EVAT (blamed for the senatorial defeats of Recto and Defensor). To critics who call the recovery a myth the poor cannot feel, he replies with 'the first of a thousand steps' (Korea, Singapore and China needed years), and closes with his cancer-patient analogy: a people who trust their leader will bear 'transitory torment' as a patient trusts a physician through chemotherapy, while a distrusted leader is mocked even for the pain of the cure -- as India's reformers found when they were voted out and their opponents reaped the prosperity. The moral: 'aspire for credibility, first and foremost.'
